cards.front: In CF, the nebulised mucolytic dornase alfa cleaves [___] DNA released from neutrophils, reducing mucus viscosity.
cards.context:
Dornase alfa is recombinant human DNase I — it digests the extracellular DNA released by dead neutrophils, which is the dominant viscosity contributor in CF mucus.

The result is thinner mucus that clears with physiotherapy. Effect builds over weeks of daily use.

cards.front: A playful, afebrile 3-year-old has a smooth mass confined to the left flank, noticed by her parents two days ago; it does not cross the midline and CT shows no calcification. The most likely diagnosis is [___].
cards.context:
Every negative is doing work: well and playful (not the systemically unwell neural-crest picture), confined to one flank without crossing the midline, no calcification, and the 3-4 year peak age.

Management trap: do not repeatedly palpate — rupture seeds the peritoneum and upstages the tumour.

cards.front: A 2-year-old with sudden coughing after a choking episode has a film showing increased [___] of the right lung field — the sign of air trapping.
cards.context:
Inhaled foreign body is the toddler-with-sudden-cough film, and the abnormality is the opposite of what students expect.

The obstructed lung is not opaque — it is too black. A ball-valve obstruction lets air in on inspiration but not out on expiration, so the lung stays inflated.

cards.front: When consent cannot be obtained in time and delay risks death or serious injury, treatment proceeds under the [___] doctrine.
cards.context:
The emergency doctrine covers treatment necessary to prevent death or serious injury when consent cannot be obtained in time. It covers what is necessary now, not everything you would eventually like to do.

Document what made it an emergency and why consent could not be obtained.

cards.front: A child develops a slowly expanding annular rash with central clearing about 10 days after a tick bite while hiking in an endemic region; the causative spirochaete is [___].
cards.context:
Erythema migrans is the pathognomonic early sign of this infection. Serology is frequently negative this early, so a lesion expanding to ≥5 cm in an exposed person is treated empirically.

The exposure is the hinge in Australia: there is no established local transmission, so the diagnosis needs travel to an endemic region (North America, Europe, parts of Asia).

A tick bite acquired here is not Lyme disease.

cards.front: Intussusception is most common from 3 months to 2 years, peaking at [___] months; classic findings include a 'sausage-shaped' RUQ mass and 'redcurrant jelly' stool (late sign of ischaemia).
cards.context:
Intussusception (bowel telescoping into an adjacent segment) is most common from 3 months to 2 years, peaking at 4-9 months.

Most ileocolic, no lead point. USS shows target sign. First-line: pneumatic or hydrostatic enema reduction; surgery if failed or unstable.

cards.front: A child with Hirschsprung disease develops fever, distension and explosive foul diarrhoea. If rectal washout is needed, it should be performed by the [___].
cards.context:
Fever, distension and explosive foul diarrhoea in a child with Hirschsprung disease indicate Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis, which can progress rapidly.

Rectal washout is not a casual ward procedure in this setting. The RCH guideline specifies that it should be performed by the surgical team while the child receives urgent assessment and treatment.

cards.front: The most common congenital heart lesion overall is VSD; the most common cyanotic congenital lesion presenting *after* the neonatal period is [___].
cards.context:
Ventricular septal defect (VSD) is the most common CHD overall — a left-to-right shunt. Cyanotic lesions are less common but more dramatic.

Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) is the commonest cyanotic CHD overall. Timing depends on RV outflow obstruction: severe TOF may be cyanotic at birth, while milder “pink” TOF may become cyanotic later.

Transposition of the great arteries (TGA) is commonest in the first week — ductal-dependent for mixing.

cards.front: An exclusively breastfed, thriving 8-week-old has a haemoglobin of 96 g/L; the identical value in a 3-year-old would be frank anaemia. At this age it is the expected physiological nadir and needs no [___].
cards.context:
An eight-week-old sits precisely at the physiological trough, so a haemoglobin near 96 g/L in a thriving, feeding baby is expected rather than pathological.

The same value in a three-year-old, whose floor is 110 g/L, is unambiguous anaemia and needs a cause. What distinguishes them is the age, not the number — which is why the reflex treatment here would be wrong.

Look instead for the features that make it NOT physiological: poor growth, prematurity, blood loss, or a trough that fails to recover by four to six months.

cards.front: The tympanic membrane finding that distinguishes acute otitis media from otitis media with effusion is that it is [___].
cards.context:
An effusion alone is not otitis media. Both conditions show fluid behind the drum, so the discriminator has to be a sign of pressure and acute inflammation.

Getting this right is what keeps antibiotics away from a child with a resolving effusion.

cards.front: Winter wheeze plus crackles in a first episode under 12 months is [___], not a first presentation of asthma.
cards.context:
Preschool asthma and recurrent viral wheeze need a pattern of repeated episodes.

A first winter illness under 12 months that mixes wheeze with crackles is bronchiolitis and is managed supportively, not with inhalers or steroids.

cards.front: A 2-year-old is not yet walking. Within the ADING framework, the domain that asks about prematurity and perinatal insult is [___], and establishing whether a second stream is also delayed matters because delay across two or more domains defines global developmental delay.
cards.context:
This is ADING used as a diagnostic instrument rather than recited as a checklist. A 2-year-old not yet walking is a developmental red flag, but the framework is what turns that into a differential.

The antenatal domain asks about prematurity and perinatal insult. The nutrition and growth domains ask whether this is part of faltering growth, and the immunisation domain matters for infection-related causes.

Delay in two or more streams is global delay and widens the workup, whereas isolated motor delay narrows it.

cards.front: The common congenital lesion causing a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge is a [___].
cards.context: A ventricular septal defect produces a left-to-right shunt and a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge. Small defects may close spontaneously.

cards.front: A well neonate with brief, sharply demarcated unilateral facial/body flushing that comes and goes has the benign [___] colour change — not a vascular emergency.
cards.context:
Newborn skin perfusion can look dramatic and still be normal. Transient unilateral flushing with a sharp midline cutoff in a well neonate is a vasomotor curiosity, not a stroke or infection workup by itself.

Reassure, keep warm, and reassess if the baby is unwell, persistent, or the demarcation is not clean.

cards.front: Most limping children don't need investigations; red flag is acute inability to [___]; always consider septic arthritis in severe localised joint pain with fever.
cards.context: Most limping children have benign causes (transient synovitis, minor trauma, growing pains). Red flags: complete inability to weight-bear, nocturnal pain (malignancy), systemic symptoms, duration >7 days.

cards.front: Cystic fibrosis is autosomal recessive mutation in the [___] gene; most common mutation is F508del (~70% of alleles).
cards.context:
Recessive inheritance means a child needs two faulty CFTR alleles (one from each carrier parent) to be affected — which is why CF is autosomal recessive and unaffected siblings can still be carriers.

F508del is a three-base deletion losing phenylalanine at position 508. The misfolded protein is degraded before reaching the cell surface.

It dominates the mutation pool and defines which CFTR modulators a patient can use.

cards.front: When EBV infectious mononucleosis is suspected, avoid empiric [___] because it can trigger a florid maculopapular rash.
cards.context:
An adolescent with sore throat, fever, and tender lymphadenopathy can look like bacterial tonsillitis. Amoxicillin during EBV infection can be followed by a maculopapular eruption.

The infection alone does not establish or exclude antibiotic allergy. Document the timing, morphology and severity, including any mucosal, respiratory or circulatory features.

Use the paediatric antibiotic-allergy pathway before assigning or removing a lasting allergy label; any drug challenge belongs in a controlled setting.

cards.front: In salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia, the oral mineralocorticoid added once feeds are tolerated is [___].
cards.context:
Salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia requires both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement.

Stress-dose hydrocortisone supplies mineralocorticoid activity during the acute phase; ongoing replacement is added once oral fluids are tolerated.

reference.title: Adrenal crisis and acute adrenal insufficiency

cards.front: Phototherapy converts unconjugated bilirubin to water-soluble photoisomers; uses blue light (450-460 nm); avoid as treatment if primarily [___] bilirubin is elevated.
cards.context:
Blue light at 450-460 nm converts unconjugated bilirubin into water-soluble photoisomers, especially lumirubin, which bypass hepatic conjugation.

Adverse effects: temperature instability, dehydration/loose stools, retinal injury without eye protection, and bronze baby syndrome if conjugated bilirubin is high.

cards.front: A newborn is tachypnoeic when the respiratory rate is above [___] breaths per minute.
cards.context:
Counting the rate is what separates a settling newborn from one in respiratory distress, so it is the first objective number to get.

Count for a full minute — newborn breathing is periodic, and a 15-second count extrapolated up is unreliable.

cards.front: Loss of a contiguous block of neighbouring genes, too small to see on a routine karyotype, is a [___] — the reason one lesion affects unrelated organs.
cards.context:
A microdeletion removes several neighbouring genes in a segment too small for a routine karyotype. The shared loss explains effects across unrelated organs.

The 22q11 pattern combines conotruncal heart disease, hypocalcaemia, thymic hypoplasia and palatal problems.

cards.front: A baby aged 2–8 weeks with projectile non-bilious vomiting and a palpable 'olive' has [___].
cards.context:
The hypertrophied pylorus blocks gastric outflow at 2–8 weeks.

Recognise it by projectile NON-bilious vomiting (obstruction is proximal to the bile duct) in a baby who's hungry again straight after — and a palpable 'olive'.

cards.front: The paediatric triad of polyuria, polydipsia and unexplained weight loss is [___] mellitus until proven otherwise — usually type 1.
cards.context: The classic new-onset triad in a child — polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss (sometimes with a recent enuresis relapse). Type 1 (autoimmune, insulin-deficient) dominates; check a glucose/ketones before they tip into DKA.

cards.front: The thymus undergoes temporary [___] during acute illness, with rebound regrowth after recovery or chemotherapy.
cards.context:
Thymic size changes with the child's health, which explains a film that looks different from last week's.

Temporary involution is seen during acute illness in most neonates. Rebound regrowth follows recovery from severe illness or chemotherapy.

cards.front: Slapped cheek disease is caused by [___] B19, and is followed by a lacy reticular rash on the limbs.
cards.context:
Slapped cheek disease — erythema infectiosum, or fifth disease — is caused by PARVOVIRUS B19.

The facial erythema is followed some days later by a lacy, reticular rash on the limbs that characteristically comes and goes for weeks, flaring with heat, exercise or sunlight.

That relapsing lacy rash is often mistaken for a new illness or a drug reaction, when it is the same illness waxing and waning.

cards.front: A four-year-old completely avulses an upper primary incisor. Unlike a permanent tooth, it should not be [___].
cards.context:
An avulsed permanent tooth should be replanted urgently when appropriate.

An avulsed primary tooth is not replanted because insertion can damage the developing permanent successor.

cards.front: A jaundiced newborn needs bilirubin fractionation. A raised [___] fraction points to cholestasis and requires prompt investigation.
cards.context:
Physiological neonatal jaundice is predominantly unconjugated. Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia instead suggests impaired bile flow or liver disease.

Pale stools and dark urine strengthen concern; timely evaluation is essential because biliary atresia requires early treatment.

cards.front: In NSW a young person may give their own valid consent to medical treatment from age [___], and consent from age 16 is treated as an adult's.
cards.context:
Section 49 of the Minors (Property and Contracts) Act 1970 (NSW). At 14 the young person can consent for themselves; at 16 their consent is treated as an adult's.

The section protects the doctor from a claim in battery — it does not remove the value of involving a parent where the young person agrees to that.

cards.front: In Wilson disease, copper accumulates because the liver cannot excrete it into [___].
cards.context:
The defect is failure of biliary excretion — the liver's only meaningful route for getting rid of copper. Dietary copper keeps arriving and cannot leave.

That is why treatment is lifelong: chelators pull stored copper out and zinc blocks new copper being absorbed, but nothing repairs the transporter.

cards.front: In Kawasaki disease, IVIG is ideally given during the first [___] days of illness, but later treatment may still be indicated.
cards.context:
Give IVIG promptly once indicated. Early treatment improves coronary outcomes.

IVIG should still be given after day 10 when active inflammation persists, such as fever, raised inflammatory markers or abnormal coronary arteries. Seek senior clinical guidance.

cards.front: Gilbert syndrome is caused by reduced activity of the bilirubin-conjugating enzyme [___].
cards.context:
Gilbert syndrome is reduced activity of UGT1A1, the enzyme that conjugates bilirubin — not absent activity, just less of it, which is why the jaundice is mild and comes and goes.

It becomes visible when bilirubin production rises or conjugation is stressed: fasting, an intercurrent illness, dehydration, strenuous exercise, or the run-up to exams.

Families often report the child 'goes yellow when unwell'.

cards.front: Holliday-Segar maintenance: first 10 kg = 100 mL/kg/day; second 10 kg = 50 mL/kg/day; each kg after = [___] mL/kg/day.
cards.context:
Daily Holliday-Segar maintenance uses 100/50/20 mL/kg/day for successive weight bands. For 25 kg, this gives 1600 mL/day, or about 67 mL/hour when divided by 24.

The hourly 4-2-1 rule gives 65 mL/hour for the same child. Both are accepted starting estimates, not exact unit conversions.

Adjust for illness and fluid balance; unwell children often need less than full maintenance. Isotonic fluid with glucose is usually preferred.

cards.front: Montelukast works by blocking the [___] receptor for cysteinyl leukotrienes.
cards.context:
Montelukast is a leukotriene receptor antagonist. It blocks CysLT1, the receptor for the cysteinyl leukotrienes C4, D4 and E4.

Those leukotrienes are made from arachidonic acid by 5-lipoxygenase, and they drive bronchoconstriction, mucus secretion, microvascular leak and eosinophil recruitment.

Because it is an oral tablet, it bypasses the whole inhaler-technique problem, which is its main practical attraction in a child who cannot manage a device.

cards.front: A 6-month-old constipated since the first week of life has an empty rectum on digital exam; withdrawing the finger releases an explosive gush of stool and gas. This pattern points to [___], not functional constipation.
cards.context:
Constipation dating from the first weeks of life is itself a red flag — true functional constipation typically starts later, around toilet training or diet transitions.

The rectal findings then decide the referral: a loaded rectum fits withholding; the combination here mandates suction rectal biopsy, and laxatives alone must not close the case.

cards.front: On a child's LFTs, a rise in the hepatocellular enzymes [___] and AST points to liver-cell damage, rather than blocked bile flow.
cards.context:
ALT and AST live inside hepatocytes and leak out when liver cells are injured (e.g. viral hepatitis, paracetamol overdose). A hepatocellular picture is enzyme-leak from damaged cells.

ALT is the more liver-specific of the two; AST also rises with muscle injury, so isolated AST is not always the liver.

cards.front: The commonest organism causing childhood urinary tract infection is [___].
cards.context: UTI is a leading cause of fever without focus in young children, so a urine sample is part of that workup. The dominant uropathogen is gut-derived E. coli; a clean-catch/SPA culture confirms before/with antibiotics.

cards.front: When an infantile haemangioma needs treatment (e.g. near the eye or airway), the first-line drug is oral [___].
cards.context: Treat only the minority that threaten function or ulcerate (periorbital, airway, nasal tip, large facial). Oral propranolol shrinks them — first-line over steroids/surgery.

cards.front: A nasopharyngeal airway is sized from the nostril to the [___] of the ear, and is avoided in a suspected base-of-skull fracture.
cards.context:
The nasopharyngeal airway is the adjunct for the child WITH a gag reflex — semi-conscious, obstructing, but not flat. Size it from the nostril to the tragus of the ear.

The classic contraindication is suspected base-of-skull fracture — the tube can follow the fracture line intracranially. Adenoidal bleeding is the common minor complication in children.

cards.front: After splenectomy (e.g. trauma) a child needs vaccination against the three encapsulated organisms: pneumococcus, [___], and meningococcus.
cards.context:
The same asplenia logic applies whether the spleen is autoinfarcted (sickle cell), congenitally absent, or surgically removed after trauma.

An asplenic child cannot clear encapsulated bacteria, so they need vaccination against all three plus penicillin prophylaxis.

cards.front: Before stepping up asthma therapy, check device [___] and adherence; a spacer should be used with MDIs, especially in young children.
cards.context:
Most 'uncontrolled asthma' is a technique or adherence problem, not pharmacological failure — stepping up the dose just amplifies a drug that isn't reaching the lungs.

A spacer is strongly recommended — especially in young children, who can't coordinate the actuate-and-inhale timing of a bare MDI.

The spacer holds the dose as a cloud, so slow tidal breathing delivers far more drug to the airways and less to the oropharynx.

reference.title: Asthma in primary school-aged children (6-11 years)

cards.front: A 2-year-old on oral antibiotics for acute otitis media has worsening pain, fever and swelling behind the ear that displaces the pinna [___] and forward. This is mastoiditis, which needs IV antibiotics rather than continued oral therapy.
cards.context:
Mastoiditis is the complication you are being asked to spot before it becomes intracranial, and the discriminator is where the swelling sits and what it does to the pinna.

Swelling is postero-superior to the pinna and pushes it down and forward — an appearance uncomplicated acute otitis media never produces. Progressive pain and fever despite antibiotics is the other clue.

It is mostly under 3 years, usually Strep pneumoniae, and late presentation risks meningitis, sigmoid sinus thrombosis and brain abscess.

cards.front: The Paediatric Assessment Triangle is a hands-off, [___]-the-room triage of Appearance, Work of Breathing, and Circulation to skin.
cards.context: Same PAT fact, different probe: the tool is hands-off — you read the child from the doorway before laying on hands or gadgets.

cards.front: A painful vesicular rash confined to a single dermatome that does not cross the midline is herpes [___].
cards.context: Herpes zoster is reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus in a sensory ganglion. Antivirals within 72 hours shorten the course; ophthalmic involvement (Hutchinson sign) needs urgent review.

cards.front: A 12-day-old boy with normal genitalia has vomited for three days and is now shocked. Sodium 124 mmol/L (normal 135-145), potassium 7.0 mmol/L (normal 3.5-6.0). The likely diagnosis is [___].
cards.context:
Pyloric stenosis also presents with vomiting in the first weeks of life, and the potassium separates the two.

Pyloric stenosis loses gastric acid, giving a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic alkalosis. Salt-wasting CAH lacks aldosterone, so the kidney wastes sodium and keeps potassium.

A boy's genitalia usually look normal, apart from perhaps a pigmented scrotum, so unless the newborn screen has flagged it, the electrolytes are what reveal it.

reference.title: Adrenal crisis and acute adrenal insufficiency

cards.front: A 7-year-old has deep puncture wounds on her hand from the family cat. They are irrigated in ED and look clean, and she has no allergies. The ED doctor starts oral prophylaxis with [___].
cards.context:
A cat bite, a hand bite and a deep puncture each justify prophylaxis on their own, even when the wound looks clean, and this child has all three.

Cat teeth inoculate Pasteurella multocida deep into tissue. Cefalexin, the usual skin-infection choice, covers staphylococci and streptococci but not Pasteurella.

RCH gives a 5-day oral course; follow the local protocol.

cards.front: First-line investigation for suspected IgE-mediated food allergy is [___] testing.
cards.context:
Skin prick testing introduces tiny amounts of allergen into the dermis and reads the wheal size at 15 minutes — a direct, in-vivo readout of mast-cell-bound IgE.

The key caveats: a positive test only confirms sensitisation, not clinical allergy — interpret in the context of a convincing history.

cards.front: Giving amoxicillin to someone with EBV mononucleosis classically triggers a widespread maculopapular [___].
cards.context:
A classic trap: prescribing amoxicillin (or ampicillin) for a presumed bacterial sore throat that is actually EBV can produce a florid maculopapular eruption.

Historical estimates near 90% are higher than modern series, which report the rash in a substantial minority; it is not automatically a true penicillin allergy.

cards.front: A nasogastric tube whose tip sits at or above the gastro-oesophageal junction risks reflux of feed and therefore [___].
cards.context:
The reason a high nasogastric tube is dangerous, not just untidy.

Feed delivered at or above the gastro-oesophageal junction refluxes straight back up the oesophagus, and in a supine infant with an immature airway that means aspiration.

cards.front: The commonest cause of hip pain in a well preschooler after a recent viral illness is transient [___].
cards.context: The benign, common one — but always a diagnosis made only after excluding septic arthritis. A well child, often just after a viral URTI, with a transiently irritable hip that settles in 1–2 weeks.

cards.front: The sickle mutation replaces [___] with valine at position 6 of the β-globin chain.
cards.context:
A single base change in the β-globin gene (HBB) swaps a charged residue for a hydrophobic one.

On deoxygenation the abnormal haemoglobin polymerises into rigid fibres that deform the red cell into the classic sickle shape.

cards.front: A 4-year-old with thrombocytopenia has pallor, bone pain and hepatosplenomegaly. Before treating presumed ITP, the paediatrician urgently reviews a [___] for blasts.
cards.context:
Isolated ITP occurs in an otherwise well child. Bone pain, pallor and organomegaly raise concern for a marrow disorder such as leukaemia.

Review the full blood count and blood film before ITP treatment. Abnormal cells or these clinical red flags need urgent paediatric or haematology assessment.

cards.front: A 3-year-old girl has painless vaginal bleeding and a soft grape-like mass protruding from the introitus. The diagnosis is [___].
cards.context: Sarcoma botryoides is a botryoid embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma of the vagina, usually presenting before age 5. Painless bleeding or a grape-like mass needs urgent oncological assessment.

cards.front: A well 4-year-old has two small, weeping patches under one nostril topped with honey-coloured crusts, and no lesions elsewhere. The GP's first treatment, three times daily, is topical [___].
cards.context:
Honey-coloured crusts on a red, weeping base are impetigo, from group A streptococcus or Staphylococcus aureus. A few small lesions can be treated on the skin alone.

Widespread or large lesions need an oral antibiotic instead, and RCH uses cefalexin.

Cover the sores and keep the child out of childcare until treatment has started, because school sores spread easily.

cards.front: Beta thalassaemia major drives compensatory extramedullary haematopoiesis with frontal bossing, maxillary hyperplasia, and [___].
cards.context:
Absent beta chains in beta thalassaemia major leave alpha chains unpaired and red cells fragile.

The bone marrow expands to compensate, producing frontal bossing and maxillary hyperplasia ('chipmunk facies'); extramedullary haematopoiesis enlarges the liver and spleen.

Transfusion-dependent from ~6 months when HbF production ceases.

cards.front: The first-line antibiotic for acute otitis media, when one is indicated, is [___].
cards.context:
Most AOM is viral and self-limiting, so many cases are simply observed.

When antibiotics are indicated because of age, systemic illness, persistent or severe symptoms, complications or high-risk status, amoxicillin is first-line; use the local antimicrobial guideline.

Bilateral disease under 2 may lower the treatment threshold but is not an automatic indication under Australian RCH guidance.

cards.front: An unresponsive 4-month-old lies supine in the resuscitation bay, her large occiput pushing her chin towards her chest. Before bag-mask ventilation, the ED registrar places her head in the [___] position.
cards.context:
An infant's large occiput flexes the neck when supine, and the soft, pliable trachea kinks if the head is pushed back too far.

So infants under 1 year are held neutral with the jaw supported, while older children move into the sniffing position.

If the airway is still obstructed, add a jaw thrust or a very slight extra tilt rather than full extension.

cards.front: Otitis externa affects the ear canal; cardinal clinical sign is pain when pulling the [___] or pressing the tragus — distinguishes it from otitis media, which affects the middle ear.
cards.context:
Otitis externa is a skin/soft-tissue infection of the external auditory canal — distinct from otitis media (middle ear behind intact TM).

Cardinal sign: pain on pulling pinna or pressing tragus (moves inflamed canal skin) — AOM doesn't cause this.

Topical antibiotic + steroid drops (Sofradex, Ciproxin HC); DON'T syringe (risks pushing infection deeper).

cards.front: Christmas disease is [___] (Factor IX), not the commoner Factor VIII form.
cards.context: Christmas disease is the Factor IX deficiency. It is five times rarer than Factor VIII deficiency, same X-linked inheritance, same prolonged aPTT.

cards.front: Nebulised hypertonic saline (~[___]%) is used in CF to rehydrate airway surface liquid; pre-treat with salbutamol to prevent reflex bronchoconstriction.
cards.context:
Hypertonic saline (6-7%) draws water into the airway lumen by osmosis, rehydrating the surface liquid that CFTR dysfunction has dehydrated.

Pre-treat with a bronchodilator — the osmotic load can trigger reflex bronchoconstriction.

cards.front: Under RCH criteria, complete Kawasaki disease can be diagnosed after at least [___] days of fever with sufficient characteristic clinical features.
cards.context:
RCH complete-disease criteria require fever for at least four days and at least four principal clinical features at any point during the illness, with no alternative explanation. The features need not be simultaneous.

Suspected incomplete disease needs assessment using its separate pathway; do not wait for a mandatory fifth day.

cards.front: Kernicterus = irreversible [___] encephalopathy from the unconjugated form crossing the blood-brain barrier and depositing in the basal ganglia; chronic sequelae include choreoathetoid cerebral palsy and sensorineural hearing loss.
cards.context:
Kernicterus is irreversible bilirubin encephalopathy — unconjugated bilirubin crosses the blood-brain barrier, deposits in basal ganglia, and causes neurological damage.

Chronic sequelae: choreoathetoid cerebral palsy, sensorineural hearing loss, dental enamel hypoplasia.

Risk factors lower the threshold: prematurity, sepsis, acidosis, hypoalbuminaemia (less protein binding).

cards.front: Night terrors occur in the first third of the night, whereas nightmares arise out of [___] sleep.
cards.context:
The distinction is made on timing and recall, not on how frightening the episode looked to the parent.

A child wakes from a nightmare, can be consoled, and remembers it. A child in a night terror does not truly wake and recalls nothing.

cards.front: When assessing possible dehydration in an infant, compare fluid intake and urine output with the child's [___].
cards.context: Compare drinking, feeds and urine output with the child's usual pattern. Reduced urine output supports dehydration assessment, but a nappy count alone cannot grade the fluid deficit.

cards.front: Early introduction of allergenic foods (peanut, egg) via oral route promotes tolerance before transcutaneous sensitisation; supported by LEAP and [___] studies.
cards.context:
The skin barrier hypothesis: cutaneous (eczema-mediated) exposure primes Th2 sensitisation; oral exposure promotes tolerance. LEAP means Learning Early About Peanut Allergy; EAT means Enquiring About Tolerance.

 These trials informed the shift away from delaying common food allergens. Australian guidelines now recommend introduction at around 6 months, when the infant is developmentally ready, rather than delay.

cards.front: HUS triad: microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (schistocytes, raised LDH, low haptoglobin), [___] (consumed in microthrombi), and acute kidney injury. Typical (D+) HUS follows bloody diarrhoea from Shiga-toxin-producing *E. coli*.
cards.context:
HUS (haemolytic uraemic syndrome) triad: microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (schistocytes on film, raised LDH, low haptoglobin), thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury (rising creatinine, oliguria).

Typical (D+ HUS) follows bloody diarrhoea from Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (O157:H7); 5-10 days latency.

Treatment is supportive — antibiotics may worsen disease.

cards.front: A child in shock with delayed capillary refill needs 10–20 mL/kg boluses of isotonic [___], reassessed after each.
cards.context:
Shock in children is compensated until late — tachycardia and poor perfusion precede hypotension.

Resuscitation means repeated 10–20 mL/kg isotonic fluid boluses with reassessment after each; maintenance fluids come later.

cards.front: Management of bronchiolitis in an infant under 12 months is essentially [___] — salbutamol, steroids and antibiotics are not recommended and do not change the disease course.
cards.context:
Bronchiolitis causes small-airway oedema, epithelial debris and mucus plugging. Management is supportive, with oxygen, hydration and feeding support when indicated.

Beta-2 agonists are not used routinely because trials show no consistent improvement in admission, illness duration or length of stay — not because infants lack airway smooth muscle.

Corticosteroids and antibiotics also do not alter uncomplicated viral bronchiolitis.

cards.front: Per the Australian Child Maltreatment Study, about 6 in 10 children experience maltreatment; the commonest single type is exposure to domestic violence; health professionals are [___] reporters in all Australian jurisdictions.
cards.context:
The Australian Child Maltreatment Study (2023, n=8,503) found ~62% of children experience at least one of five maltreatment types.

By population prevalence the commonest is exposure to domestic violence (~40%); neglect is the LEAST common (~9%). The older 'neglect most common' figure came from notification data, not prevalence.

Health professionals are mandatory reporters in all states/territories. Threshold = REASONABLE concern: flag, don't investigate or prove abuse.

cards.front: Strabismus affects ~2% of children; untreated risks [___] (vision suppression in the misaligned eye).
cards.context:
Strabismus (eye misalignment) affects ~2% of children. Risk factors: family history, prematurity, refractive error (commonly hyperopia → accommodative esotropia), neurological disorders.

Untreated strabismus causes amblyopia (vision suppression in the misaligned eye) — refer to ophthalmology by age 4-6 months for any persistent misalignment.

cards.front: Hyaline membrane disease is prevented with antenatal steroids given to the mother and treated with exogenous [___] instilled via the endotracheal tube.
cards.context:
Treatment follows directly from the mechanism, and both halves are examinable.

Antenatal corticosteroids given to the mother accelerate fetal surfactant production. Exogenous surfactant is then instilled after birth down the endotracheal tube.

cards.front: In a low-risk child, the fever minor criterion for acute rheumatic fever needs a documented temperature of at least [___] °C.
cards.context:
High-risk children need only 38 °C, a lower cut-off the guideline adopts because it improves sensitivity for ARF in those groups.

In high-risk groups a reliable history of fever can also count when antipyretic medication has already masked the temperature.

cards.front: In the MTA trial for core ADHD symptoms (inattention, hyperactivity, impulsivity), the single key active treatment ingredient was [___]; adding behavioural therapy gave extra benefit only for non-core symptoms (anxiety, aggression).
cards.context:
The MTA trial (Multimodal Treatment of ADHD, NIMH) randomised children to medication, behaviour therapy, combined, or community care.

Combined therapy was best for non-core symptoms (anxiety, aggression, social skills, parent-child relationships).

cards.front: Before stepping up asthma therapy, check device technique and adherence; a [___] should be used with MDIs, especially in young children.
cards.context:
Most 'uncontrolled asthma' is a technique or adherence problem, not pharmacological failure — stepping up the dose just amplifies a drug that isn't reaching the lungs.

A spacer is strongly recommended — especially in young children, who can't coordinate the actuate-and-inhale timing of a bare MDI.

The spacer holds the dose as a cloud, so slow tidal breathing delivers far more drug to the airways and less to the oropharynx.

reference.title: Asthma in primary school-aged children (6-11 years)

cards.front: Monospot test for EBV is rapid and [___] but lacks sensitivity — false negatives common in first week and in children under 4; send VCA-IgM serology if Monospot negative and suspicion remains high.
cards.context:
Monospot detects heterophile antibodies — IgM that EBV infection induces against unrelated antigens (horse RBCs in the test).

Sensitivity is poor — false negatives in the first week (antibodies not yet developed) and in children under 4 (humoral response often skips heterophile stage).

cards.front: The commonest enzyme defect causing episodic haemolysis in children, often triggered by infection, fava beans, or certain drugs, is [___].
cards.context:
G6PD (glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase) protects red cells from oxidative stress; without it, an oxidant trigger makes them haemolyse, often with bite cells and Heinz bodies on film.

It is X-linked, so boys are affected far more than girls — a key paediatric clue.

cards.front: A white pupillary reflex (leukocoria) in a child must be treated as [___] until excluded.
cards.context:
A white pupillary reflex (instead of red) is never normal.

The must-exclude cause is retinoblastoma — the commonest intraocular malignancy of childhood; congenital cataract is the other key cause. Urgent ophthalmology referral.

cards.front: Leg bowing, widened wrists, and a 'rachitic rosary' from vitamin D deficiency in a child is [___].
cards.context: Rickets is defective mineralisation of growing bone, usually from vitamin D deficiency. Bloods show low or normal calcium, low phosphate, and high ALP and PTH; treat with vitamin D and calcium.
